Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Body, health & movement · Church life

kneel verb

also kneel down, kneeling, on one’s knees, go down on one’s knees, genuflect

classical

Ov. Met. 4.340: flexum genū (Lewis & Short s.v. flectō)
Sen. Herc. F. 410: inflexō genū adōrāre (Lewis & Short s.v. genū)
Vulg. Eph. 3.14

genua flectere

kneel, bend the knee

To bend the knee; kneeling is flexīs genibus, the school dialogues’ phrase for kneeling to pray (Corderius, Erasmus); Ovid and Seneca have the singular. The Orthodox churches keep the rule of the Council of Nicaea (canon 20) that on Sundays and from Easter to Pentecost prayer is made standing, until the kneeling prayers of Pentecost evening; in the Latin rite kneeling is a regular posture at Mass.

Examples

  • flectō genua mea ad Patrem Dominī nostrī Jēsū Chrīstī

    I bend my knees before the Father of our Lord Jesus ChristVulg. Eph. 3.14

  • Flexīs genibus, et conjūnctīs manibus dīxī precātiōnem Dominicam, cum grātiārum āctiōne.

    On my knees, with my hands together, I said the Lord’s Prayer and a thank-you.Cord. Coll. 1.2

  • elephantum minimus Aethiops jubet subsīdere in genua et ambulāre per fūnem

    the smallest African boy makes the elephant kneel down and walk the tightropeSen. Ep. 85.41

Other words

  • genua pōnere — kneel down

    also used · classical · Curt. 4.6.28 (Lewis & Short s.v. genū); Vulg. Lc. 22.41

    Curtius’s phrase (genū pōnere), and the Vulgate’s: positīs genibus ōrābat, he knelt down and prayed.

  • in genua subsīdere — go down on one’s knees (outside church too)

    also used · classical · Sen. Ep. 85.41

    To sink onto one’s knees, of anyone kneeling down.

See also bow, bow one’s head, fold one’s hands, pray.

SourcesLewis & Short: genu · Lewis & Short: flecto · Lewis & Short: pono · Lewis & Short: subsido
